title_original: Lunch With Adam: Met Curator Alisa LaGamma on Repatriation, the Revitalized Rockefeller Wing, the Benin Bronzes, and More
excerpt_original: 'We all need to come up with imaginative solutions moving forward.'

blocks.text: Alisa LaGamma is the Ceil and Michael E. Pulitzer Curator of the Department of the Arts of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas at the Metropolitan Museum of Art . As a lifelong collector of African art myself, I have seen many of her shows and also served on her committee for years, more recently as chairman. The history of these objects is a fascinating one, from the painful colonial era to the struggle to have this art broadly accepted in the art world. Few people realize that it wasn’t until the ’80s that the Met exhibited these artworks, and before that, many saw them as little more than artifacts. This field is currently the subject of ongoing debate regarding the politics of restitution and the complex realities of repatriation. On our return from Parcours du Monde , the classic African and Oceanic art fair in Paris, last month, and not long after the one-year anniversary of the $70 million rebuild of the entire wing, it felt timely to explore a few topics in the zeitgeist.

Adam: What is the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing? Can you explain the Met’s relationship to classic African, Oceanic, and Ancient American art?

Alisa: Sure—it’s a fascinating story. In 1969 New York’s Governor Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller and the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced that a new wing of the museum would be built in order to accept the gift of his collection of sub-Saharan Africa, Oceania, and the Ancient Americas. The collection had until then been housed at his Museum for Primitive Art.

This development fundamentally redefined the mission of the Met, which was then, as it is today, one of America’s leading museums. The move established that suddenly artistic traditions of three-quarters of the world, previously relegated to natural history museums, were to be recognized shoulder to shoulder with the then pinnacle of art history—the Old Masters of Western European art. Overnight the Met’s identity became that of a global institution whose aspiration was to represent all cultures.

Adam: It was a pretty radical move at the time—a major shift that changed the way we in the West see art from these huge regions of the world, and had a big impact on collectors, galleries, and museums by expanding notions of what is considered fine art. But people might not realize that the Met wasn’t on board with it at first.

Alisa: That’s right—that transformation led by Rockefeller was a hard-fought one. His enthusiasm for non-Western art was not originally shared by the Metropolitan, so actually in 1954 he established his own private institution across from the Museum of Modern Art. He was being advised by the leading specialists in what were then very young branches of art history, as he sought to assemble a survey of the major traditions absent from the Met.
Alisa LaGamma and Adam Lindemann. Photos: The Met and the author

Adam: Here’s this politician from one of the wealthiest families in the U.S., as close to American royalty as we get, and he’s asking for these objects, which were considered ethnographic material from what was then the farthest reaches of the world, to be recognized as fine art. What drove this passion of his?

Alisa: In 1930, the year Nelson graduated from Dartmouth he was made a Met trustee. The son of John D. and Abby Rockefeller, his mother had instilled in him an awareness of the important role that African and Ancient American art had played in the transformation of 20th-century art. As an internationalist and a statesman, in the years that followed he embraced learning about less familiar parts of the world through their artistic traditions. This led to his conviction that “all people have art.”

Nelson’s son, Michael, shared his father’s passion for that mission and majored in anthropology at Harvard. He was deeply and personally inspired by the cultures and art of the Pacific and pursued new avenues of inquiry into artistic practice during his travels there. We have incredibly striking Asmat sculptures he researched and collected in southwest New Guinea on view in the wing. In 1961, during his second trip to research, collect, and document the works of artists in Papua New Guinea he was in a small craft at the mouth of the Betsj River that ran out of gas and was drifting into the Arafura Sea. In attempt to swim to shore he tragically drowned.

Adam: And this is all happening in the ’60s and ’70s, when so much of the world, including the U.S., was undergoing major shifts in culture and society. How did that play into these collections coming to the Met?

Alisa: Major developments at home and abroad over the course of the 1960s relating to Civil Rights and the coming of age of new nation states across Africa were such that by 1969, Rockefeller’s campaign to incorporate non-Western art within the Met finally succeeded. In addition to the significance of the timing, the process of absorbing an existing pioneering institution into the Met was a complex one.

On a logistical level it might be considered comparable to the recent announcement of Ronald Lauder’s Neue Galerie merger . The prior Rockefeller development, however, was not simply the addition of a major private institution and epic infusion of art but one that fundamentally redefined the mission of one of America’s leading museums. It was decided that the new Met Wing would be named for Michael Rockefeller’s quest to deepen his understanding of Asmat art and over the next decade, the staff, collection, archives, and library of what had been known as the Museum of Primitive Art was transferred into the footprint of what is today the MCR Wing.
Installation view of the Arts of Africa Galleries. Photo: Bruce Schwarz

Adam: And now you’ve just last year reopened the wing after a complete renovation and rethinking of it. Of course, scholarship on art from these regions has evolved dramatically over the last few decades. But why the full renovation?

Alisa: For much of the time that the wing was under construction, Nelson Rockefeller was vice president. He died before its completion in 1982. Encompassing 40,000 square feet of galleries at what was then the southernmost frontier of the Met campus, its inaugural state-of-the-art display made minimal reference to the original cultural contexts of the works featured. Its success was such that their study blossomed in the academy and the museum’s collection expanded in new directions.

This was increasingly evident in a growing contrast between the permanent collection galleries and the groundbreaking research that we directed toward temporary exhibitions organized by the Met’s curators. It was a priority for me that those special projects that advanced deeper understanding of major traditions represented in our collection and that developed meaningful partnerships with institutions and colleagues in the regions of the world from which the works originated be reflected in the permanent collection galleries. This led me to propose a capital project to renew the Rockefeller Wing over a decade ago. A priority for my curatorial team was to reenvision our section of the museum and reintroduce the permanent collection within three independent surveys of world art that were at once grounded in history and many layers of content enriched by engagement with experts in source countries.

This is reflected in an infusion of digital content we developed to afford greater context that includes a series of three audio guides highlighting the perspectives of an international cohort of leading public intellectuals in the arts and humanities based in centers ranging from Bamako to Bogota. We also hired filmmaker Sosena Solomon to document interviews and landmarks at a dozen sites across sub-Saharan Africa featured in a series of critically acclaimed short documentaries that widen the lens on major cultural centers relevant to deeper engagement with the decontextualized works on display. That project has created all kinds of new bridges between the Met and regional partners some of which have led to signing of new memoranda of understanding, and we have followed up with a series of workshops held at museums from Gaborone to Zanzibar in which we screen the films with regional audiences.

Another important dimension of this reset is that we have leveraged the adjacencies of neighboring sections of the museum to be more meaningful. For example, the interface of the Africa galleries and those devoted to European Renaissance sculpture and decorative arts highlights works created along the coast of West Africa from the 15th century for the earliest European traders. Completed at the end of May 2025, the reinvigorated MCR Wing has shifted from its original design as a museum within a museum to a major crossroads of the museum that is at once physically and intellectually illuminated and in dialogue with adjacent galleries of Greek and Roman, European sculpture and decorative arts, and modern and contemporary art.
A horse head by a Yoruba artist from the 12th century–15th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: Met
Adam: Alisa, how long have you worked at the Metropolitan Museum?

Alisa: I have been at the museum since I was a graduate student some 31 years ago. For the last 12 of those I’ve overseen the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing and its team of specialists that I recruited to care for the three areas of the world covered by its collections. Prior to that I was simply a senior African art specialist.
Adam: You were born in Africa. Tell me how that shaped your interest in studying African art?

Alisa: My father was an American diplomat who spent his career in both Africa and Europe. He had a deep love for the many places he worked in across sub-Saharan Africa and I was born in Lubumbashi in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and spent formative years in Zambia, Côte d’Ivoire, and Togo. My family was living in Senegal, Nigeria, and South Africa when I was in college and graduate school, the period I was myself increasingly turning my focus to art history and African art.

Adam: We recently attended the annual African and Oceanic Art Fair in Paris called Parcours du Monde (“Trip Around the World”) along with a group of friends of the Met. While there we saw all the dealers and went to both the Louvre’s Cinq Continents wing and the Quai Branly Museum for world art. I thought the most interesting and provocative part of the trip was when we went to Brussels to the Royal Museum for Central Africa at Tervuren. I’ve been enjoying African art since my late 20s, and I’ve read about Belgium’s violent colonial history in King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild. Still, only then did it strike me that we’re in 2026, and they’re still sitting on thousands of objects, things taken or stolen by King Leopold II’s privateers when it was the “Congo Free State.”

Alisa: Tervuren is a unique vestige of the European colonial presence in Africa and one of its darkest chapters. It is an institution that was essentially created as a showcase for the wealth and rich natural resources of the vast territory of Central Africa to which King Leopold of the Belgians had laid claim.
Adam: In what year was this?

Alisa: This was in the late 1800s, 1898 following the temporary colonial exhibition featured at the 1897 Brussels International Exposition. It was a branch of Leopold’s propaganda. It’s not, and was never conceived of, as an art museum. It was really an institution that showcased the minerals, the woods, the wildlife, the sheer wealth of its resources. The artifacts at Tervuren reflect decades and decades of Belgian presence in that region. Many of them were things that Belgians brought back with them, after their tours of duty and then either sold to Tervuren or transferred as gifts. There were all kinds of people coming back from the Congo. You had missionaries as well as individuals who had been part of military campaigns. Some were just pure administrators, so it’s an assemblage of artifacts that reflect the Belgian presence there over an extended period of time and the result of different interactions between Belgians and residents of this region of Central Africa. Many were very violent and brutal, some of them were more benign, but it’s an especially traumatic past. Joseph Conrad was witness to the early years of the Congo Free State and he channeled his observations in the powerful critique of European colonialism that is Heart of Darkness .
Ùhúnmwèlaò (commemorative portrait) by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 16th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met

Adam: We were looking at that amazing Kongo power figure with all those ribbons on it and that gripping face. It’s an incredible masterpiece, with a story. The military privateer Alexandre Delcommune attacked chief Ne Kuko over tariffs owed when goods were coming through their regions. The dispute was about the amount charged for passage. The people’s magical fetish was confiscated. Ne Kuko wanted it back. Delcommune refused to give it back, and eventually it ends up at Tervuren. He had seized their idol, but why did he give it to Tervuren? Why didn’t he just keep it?

Alisa: He was an unregulated tradesman taking the law into his own hands in response to tariffs that were going to be introduced and levied against him. He was outraged by that and he wanted to throw his weight around. Having spent time in the region, understanding the efficacy of that object and that it had a very important psychological role in the arbitration and adjudication of cases, his seizure of it was the ultimate way of diminishing the authority of local officials. I can’t imagine that somebody like that cared about holding on to the work. It was the removal that counted as far as he was concerned.

One of the ironies of an institution like Tervuren is that we have these stories, very detailed histories of the role specific works performed in their original communities. We know a lot about the identity of this sculpture before it was removed and that in and of itself is an incredibly important piece of historical documentation. This work which is such an incredible tour de force visually is also the materialization of a conflict. The Tervuren collection can teach us so many lessons as a result of this. These are very, very precious records that shouldn’t sit in obscurity. It really should be material that is more widely accessible, and that gives us a deeper understanding of what unfolded historically.
Adam: And that raises the obvious question: What happens now? What should museums do with these collections?

Alisa: That is precisely where provenance research and sustained dialogue with colleagues and communities connected to these works become so important. At the Met, that research has long been embedded in our curatorial practice, with specialist expertise in the field developed over more than 25 years. There isn’t necessarily a single answer that applies to every object or every collection. Belgium has passed legislation concerning existing state collections and is in active discussions with the Democratic Republic of the Congo around cultural heritage and restitution that raise larger questions about access, conservation, scholarship and where works can be most meaningfully encountered. What is essential is that these histories are researched and made transparent, and that the institutions and communities most closely connected to the material are part of determining what comes next.
Iyọ́bà (queen mother) figure by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 18th century, on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met

Adam: Simply saying “send everything back” doesn’t capture the complexity nor the realities. You’re talking about an enormous country, different communities, different histories and thousands of individual objects.

Alisa: Those questions need to be worked through collaboratively rather than answered abstractly. In doing so we should not lose sight of the importance of the works themselves as cultural achievements to be respected and honored as cultural achievements.

And in a way, that brings us back to what we were talking about with the Rockefeller Wing. Museums inherited ways of collecting, categorizing and presenting works that were products of particular moments in history. Our responsibility now is to examine those histories openly, to deepen the scholarship, to deepen the presentation of the significance of specific works, and to strengthen relationships with colleagues and communities in the places where these works originated. The museum shouldn’t obscure complexity. It should help people understand it.

Adam: There’s a real effort now to reckon with the histories of these objects and, where appropriate, to return them. My view on all these things and more is that we can’t wind back the clock—we have to find a way forward. Where do we go from here?

Alisa: We all need to come up with imaginative solutions moving forward. This month we announced a three-way agreement in which an American philanthropist who has been a longtime supporter of African art at the Met is transferring her legal title to three historical masterpieces created in what is today Nigeria to its National Commission of Museums and Monuments, which is in turn loaning the works to the Met for at least 25 years so they may be studied and experienced here in New York City. These are now on view in the Rockefeller Wing, and this fall we’re looking forward to hopefully welcoming back the director general of the NCMM, Olugbile Holloway, who joined us for the opening of the wing last year and has been a steadfast partner in this work together.

Objects have circulated, and people have circulated to define the world that we live in today. Since the end of the 19th century when these objects were traded or removed from their places of origin, the world has fundamentally changed by diasporas. Our communities are highly cosmopolitan and comprised of people from all over. And so, our institutions also reflect that. There are many historically tragic events that may be a part of the path of works of art. We shouldn’t shy away from those stories. We’re not going to reverse what happened, but we can help people understand what unfolded. In my experience, communities we have had the opportunity to represent are enormously proud of their participation. Telling those stories should heighten our sensitivity to wrongs that were done and should equip us to be more compassionate and committed to not perpetuating further damage. Museums can be places where you just go to look at beautiful things, but they should also be places where you learn about dimensions of human history that you might not be exposed to in the classroom as part of your traditional education. They’re a portal to other dimensions of how interconnected we all are, both in the past and in the present.
Body mask by Asmat artist(s), mid-20th century. Photo: The Met

Adam: How about the famous Benin bronzes. Andrea Emelife is the curator of the new Museum of West African Art in Nigeria. Many of the Benin bronzes were taken by the British army in 1897 in what is called the “Punitive Expedition.” The museum sought to get many of them back to Nigeria and built a museum for them as well as other Art. When international museums started sending back certain works, the Oba (king) of Benin appeared and sought ownership of the works. Given his family’s ancestral ownership of the objects, it becomes even more complicated to unwind the situation. What’s the fallout of that Benin story and what happens now?

Alisa: Benin art is one of the world’s great art traditions. Those works were produced in parallel to works that were created in Europe during the Renaissance. They were created by artists who had a mastery of the same technology as Donatello, Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, and Cellini. They tell a story that you cannot tell with other traditions from sub-Saharan Africa because, given that they were composed of durable materials of cast metal and carved ivory, we have exemplars of creations from this tradition going back to the 14th century, which is not the case for much of the rest of the sub-continent. For African American cultural historians like Alain Locke and W.E.B. Du Bois, an awakening to the existence of Benin art was critical to their understanding of what defined their identity, and to their writing about an African heritage.

We have very important holdings of that material because, during the late 1950s through 1960s, Nelson Rockefeller wanted to put together a collection of masterpieces. He bought the works that are now icons of the Met’s African art collection on the art market—from art dealers and at auctions. These were works that had circulated over the past generations.
Adam: Yes, but the Met gave back a few, I recall.

Alisa: In 2021, the Met voluntarily returned two Benin works from the collection to Nigeria and helped facilitate the return of a third work from an outside collector, after our collaborative research determined that the Met did not (or could not) have proper title. And that effort led to a real blossoming of partnership between the Met and Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments. We have since entered into an ongoing collaboration outlined in a memorandum of understanding that now includes the long-term project to facilitate the digitization and cataloguing of the NCMM’s collections together with a Nigerian team. And the new loan agreement I mentioned earlier builds on this foundation in a really powerful way.
Adam: Klaus Perls, Calder’s dealer, gave a lot of these works to the Met. Where did he get them from?

Alisa: Yes, the majority of the works in our collection from the Court of Benin were given by Klaus Perls. He was a major dealer of modern art who had immigrated to New York from Germany and his private passion was collecting art from the Kingdom of Benin. He gave his collection to the Metropolitan in 1991. At that time, the Metropolitan did provenance research, which is an area of research that has continued to advance significantly over the past few decades; exhibited the collection; toured it internationally; and published the works and their histories online.

The works in our collection are now displayed in our new wing, contextualized within our survey of major artistic movements and living traditions from across the subcontinent. The new presentation is grounded in contemporary research and exchanges with a network of experts at the Met and around the world, including, importantly, the voices and input of experts from Nigeria, which can all be read and heard by visitors right in the galleries alongside these works.

The day we opened the wing was the museum’s highest single-day attendance since before the pandemic. And the works are widely available not just to our more than six million yearly visitors, but also to an even larger number of people on our website and ultimately, they’re accessible to a global audience. When we reopened, we welcomed General Director Holloway and many partners and scholars from across the regions who we worked with on the display, and it was an incredibly powerful moment to celebrate culture, community, and collaboration. And we’ve also heard from many, many New Yorkers whose heritage this is who deeply appreciated seeing their culture celebrated here in New York City.
Chief Omas, Drum, mid-20th century. Photo: The Met
Adam: There’s a built-in injustice because all these things are in museums, but if you go back to the country that actually created them, you can’t find them.

Alisa: Nigeria has had among the largest holdings of Benin art even before all this transfer of works in the last couple of years. It has enormous national collections. They have not been visible because of issues with the museum’s infrastructure.

A huge part of our work together with Nigeria has been around supporting their capacity needs. Five years ago, we had a heart to heart with our counterparts in Nigeria and we asked them what is it that they felt we could be most helpful with. They responded that they didn’t have a digital collection database. So, we’ve been investing in creating a pilot for one with them and beginning the process of photographic documentation accompanied with accession records—the goal will be for the tens of thousands of works of incomparable importance in their collection to become part of that database over time.

We have the responsibility to help by being true partners, supporting the training of museum professionals and engaging in meaningful exchanges. For example, we host residencies in my department and periodically co-organize workshops with colleagues in institutions from Lagos to Gaborone and Dar es Salaam.

Adam: American museums are very different from European museums. Every situation in the art world is kind of a unique situation. For example, some of these European collections were built with works collected by the colonizing forces—unlike U.S. museums, which were built by collectors buying objects on the open market. I don’t think most people are aware when the first African show in Europe happened. Was 1920 the first time that African art had a show in the Louvre? When I learned this, I thought it was wonderful that the museum was acknowledging the influence of African abstraction and African art in the contemporary art of that time. I later found out this was just a colonial flex. This was to show how powerful France was, and that they possess all these exotic trophies. That’s the same with the British Museum. The sun never sets on the British Empire, and so for them to collect these cultural talismans, and monuments, and treasures from other places just showed how powerful they were. On the one hand, those actions are wrong, but on the other hand, perhaps if not for them, none of these things would have been preserved.

Alisa: I think we tend to oversimplify the nature of those institutions. On the one hand they are a legacy of periods in history when things were being appropriated, stolen, and looted. They’re also a part of the period in history when people are engaged in expanded networks of exchanges and trying to understand the world outside themselves. It’s the start of intellectual curiosity and scholarship concerning traditions outside of Europe, and we know so much today about what came before because of what was collected in the 18th and 19th centuries.

We don’t want to over glorify the Enlightenment period, but it is a fact that the world became a smaller place as a result. This is true with all kinds of museum collections that are diversifying and expanding. Museums are living institutions that reflect the passions of their societies. It’s incredible that in 1870 people in New York City decided to create an institution where they could learn about the world at large by assembling what is today the Metropolitan. It’s a reflection of people’s curiosity about the world outside of what they’re immediately familiar with, and their desire to experience it.

This is a very honorable intention that we shouldn’t just put to the side. It really is about sensitizing people to a more complicated world than the one that they’re immediately aware of. That’s an important thing, especially in the moment that we are living in, where we are a multicultural society in a globally interdependent world. It’s important and invaluable for us to understand diversity and the many traditions that define us. Museums have a responsibility to inspire us to learn about and respect cultures that appear to be foreign and relatively inaccessible to us. Ideally they are a springboard to venture beyond their walls and go to the source ourselves.
